fields.h1: William Carey: The Father of Modern Missions
fields.meta_title: William Carey: The Father of Modern Missions
fields.description: A self-taught shoemaker who awakened a sleeping church to the Great Commission and launched the modern missionary movement. The life of William Carey.
fields.body_html:
In the late eighteenth century, a poor English shoemaker with almost no formal education became convinced of something most Christians of his day had forgotten: that Jesus’ command to make disciples of all nations was still binding, and that the church was obliged to carry the gospel to peoples who had never heard it. That shoemaker was William Carey, and the conviction he acted on launched the modern missionary movement. He has been rightly called the “Father of Modern Missions,” not because he was the first missionary — the church had always sent some — but because he awakened a sleeping church to its duty and set in motion a wave of gospel expansion that would reach the whole world. His life is a stirring testimony to what God can do through one ordinary person who takes the Great Commission seriously: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19).

The cobbler with a map on his wall

Carey was born in 1761 in a humble English village and apprenticed as a shoemaker. Largely self-taught, he taught himself several languages while mending shoes, and he hung a homemade map of the world on his workshop wall, marking on it what he could learn about the peoples of each land and their spiritual condition. As he read of distant nations without the gospel, a burden grew in him that would not let him rest.

In Carey’s day, a deadening view had taken hold in parts of the church: that if God wished to save the heathen, he would do so without human help. When the young Carey raised the subject of foreign missions among his fellow ministers, he was reportedly told to sit down — that his enthusiasm was misguided, and that God needed no help from him to convert the nations. It was a stinging rebuff, and it reflected a fatalism that had quietly crept into the church and dulled its sense of mission. But the very fact that Carey pressed the point in the face of such discouragement shows the strength of the conviction burning in him. But Carey could not shake the plain words of Scripture: “how are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent?” (Romans 10:14–15). The command of Christ and the need of the nations pressed on him until he had to act.

Expect great things; attempt great things

In 1792 Carey published a small but revolutionary book arguing that Christians were obligated to use every means to spread the gospel to all nations, dismantling the excuses of his generation one by one. That same year he preached a sermon that became a rallying cry for a movement. From the promise of Isaiah that God’s people should “enlarge the place of your tent” and “spread abroad to the right and to the left” (Isaiah 54:2–3), Carey drew two unforgettable challenges: Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God.

Those words lit a fire. A missionary society was formed, and the following year Carey himself sailed for India with his family, becoming the first of a great army of workers who would follow. He put his own life where his preaching had been, refusing to ask others to go where he would not go himself. He believed the promise that “the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord as the waters cover the sea” (Habakkuk 2:14), and he gave his life to help make it so.

Decades of patient, plodding labour

Carey’s years in India were marked by hardship, discouragement, and staggering perseverance. He buried a child, watched his wife’s health collapse, saw his early labours meet little visible fruit, and once lost years of priceless manuscript work to a warehouse fire — only to begin again. Yet he pressed on for over forty years without a furlough home. Asked the secret of his success, he is said to have replied that he could plod; he could persevere in any definite pursuit. His genius, he insisted, was simply the refusal to give up.

And the fruit, over time, was immense. Carey and his colleagues translated the Bible, in whole or in part, into dozens of the languages of India and beyond — an achievement of astonishing scale that put the Scriptures within reach of hundreds of millions who had never had them in their own tongue. When one considers that Carey began as an unschooled cobbler, the linguistic labour alone is staggering; he mastered language after language and laboured over grammars and dictionaries that scholars would use for generations. He counted the toil worthwhile because he believed every people had a right to hear God speak in their own language, and that faith comes by hearing the word of Christ. He established schools, fought against social evils, promoted the printing of Scripture, and laid foundations that others would build on for generations. He embodied the resolve of the sower who “goes out weeping, bearing the seed for sowing,” trusting that he would “come home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves with him” (compare Psalm 126:6).

A reformer as well as a preacher

Carey understood that the gospel speaks to the whole of life, and his labours in India ranged far beyond preaching and translation. Settling with his colleagues at Serampore, he helped build a remarkable community of missionaries who worked, prayed, and pooled their resources together for the cause. He founded a college for training Indian Christians, established a printing press that poured out Scripture and literature, and became a respected scholar of India’s languages and even a professor.

He also set himself against social evils with the same tenacity he brought to everything. He laboured for years against the practice of burning widows alive and against the killing of infants, gathering evidence, appealing to the authorities, and rejoicing when such practices were at last outlawed. He promoted agriculture, education, and the study of India’s own literature, believing that love for a people meant seeking their good in every sphere. In all of it, Carey modelled a missionary vision that honoured the people he served and sought their flourishing in body as well as soul.

What made him a father of missions

Carey’s greatest legacy was not any single achievement but the movement he set in motion. Before him, Protestant missions to the wider world were rare and scattered; after him, they became a great and organized endeavour, as society after society was founded and worker after worker went out. He gave the church back its confidence in the Great Commission and showed that ordinary believers, banded together and trusting God, could reach the nations.

He also modelled how missions should be done — with deep respect for the languages and cultures of the peoples he served, with a commitment to translating the Scriptures so that every people could read God’s word in their own tongue, and with a long-term patience that expected fruit in God’s time. His life answered the call of the risen Christ: “Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation” (Mark 16:15), and “you will be my witnesses... to the end of the earth” (Acts 1:8).

His enduring challenge

William Carey died in India in 1834, having spent his whole adult life for the gospel among a people not his own. He asked that his gravestone bear only his name, his dates, and a line from a hymn describing himself as a poor, weak, and helpless worm on whom God had shown kindness — a humility striking in a man of such achievement. He knew that whatever had been accomplished was God’s doing, not his own, and he wanted the world to see grace rather than genius when it remembered him.

Carey’s life still challenges the church to lift its eyes to the fields, which are “white for harvest” (John 4:35), and to declare God’s glory “among the nations” (Psalm 96:3). His example asks every believer whether we truly expect great things from God, and whether we are willing to attempt great things for him. Most of us will not cross oceans as Carey did, but all of us are called to care that the nations know Christ, and to play our part — by going ourselves, by giving generously, by praying earnestly, by sending and upholding others — in the great work he did so much to begin. From a cobbler’s bench came a movement that has carried the gospel to the ends of the earth, and it is not finished yet. Carey’s watchword still rings across the centuries to every believer who dares to take God at his word: expect great things from God, and attempt great things for him. The God who used a poor and unschooled shoemaker to reach a whole continent is able to use any life laid at his feet — and he still calls labourers into a harvest that remains as plentiful as ever.
